item.title: [8] Variational Optimal Control for Diffusion Guidance
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Derives inference-time diffusion guidance and reward adaptation from one variational control principle (Doob transform, Jacobian pullback) with a distilled variant, directly relevant to the guidance machinery you use for steering structure models with experimental data.

Ruoyu Wang, Xinyi Ye, Yunshuo Shi, Liangyu Yuan, Beier Zhu, Chi Zhang

arXiv:2610.37146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a variational control framework that connects sampling-time guidance and reward-based model adaptation through a shared Jacobian pullback. Starting from terminal reward maximization with a path-space KL penalty, the Gibbs variational principle and Doob transform yield a correction to the generative dynamics. A local denoising approximation exposes the pullback that transports output preferences to the controlled variable. This construction gives Variational Optimal Guidance (VOG) in state space and extends to Distilled Variational Optimal Control (DVOC) by amortizing locally improved endpoints into model parameters. The resulting controls share a local variational rule: VOG acts through the denoising Jacobian, while DVOC realizes the parameter pullback by endpoint distillation. Under a linear MMSE model, VOG's exact correction lies in the data subspace. On ImageNet, VOG reduces DiT-XL/2 FID from 2.27 to 2.04 at 250 sampling steps and from 7.58 to 4.44 at 25 steps. After 20 updates on Z-Image-Turbo, DVOC improves HPSv3++ and four held-out evaluator scores over the untrained model, with the highest corresponding means among the trained methods compared. These results connect inference-time control and reward adaptation through a common geometric principle.

item.title: [8] Neopep: Reinforcement Learning From Machine-Learned Force Field Energy for Non-Canonical Peptide Structure Prediction
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

Neopep fine-tunes a diffusion structure predictor with RL against a machine-learned force field energy, which is a reward-guidance approach to cofolding-style models that you should look at closely, although the target is ncAA peptides rather than experimental data.

Jagannathan, D., Kim, P. M.

Peptide therapeutics occupy a compelling middle ground between small molecules and larger proteins, and in practice, most approved peptide drugs incorporate non-canonical amino acids (ncAAs) or other non-peptidic chemistries to elicit improved physiochemical properties (Yaseen Khan et al. (2026)). The chemical space of known ncAAs numbers in the thousands, yet current state-of-theart sequence-to-structure prediction models handle them poorly, because fewer than 0.02% of residues deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) (Berman et al. (2003)), the main source of training data, correspond to ncAAs. Our central idea is that this data bottleneck can be overcome by coupling generative structure prediction with reinforcement learning (RL) from machine-learned force field (MLFF)-derived energy. We present Neopep, a sequence-conditioned diffusion model for ncAA-containing peptide structure prediction, first pretrained on PDB structures to establish a structural prior and then fine-tuned via RL: for ncAAcontaining peptide sequences, the model proposes structures that are scored by a frozen MLFF, and this energy signal is backpropagated directly into the model to progressively lower the energy of its predictions. MLFFs have demonstrated near-quantum accuracy across much of chemical space, approacing DFT-level accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost (Kabylda et al. (2025)). This makes them substantially more accurate than classical, empirically derived force fields, which are parametrised for the canonical 20 amino acids and do not generalise to arbitrary chemistries. While Neopep is trained on a fixed set of 189 ncAAs, the underlying architecture operates at atom-level granularity and is in principle generalisable to any chemistry. We show that our model is able to produce structures of ncAA-containing peptides that achieve lower RMSD values on average to the ground truth structures, in comparison to without finetuning and other state-of the-art structure prediction models.

item.title: [7] Structure, Not Sequence: Tracking and Validating Folding Mechanisms in ESMFold's Trunk with Sparse Autoencoders
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Sparse autoencoders on the ESMFold folding trunk show that pair representations compute pairwise geometry and that concept activations forecast fold quality, which speaks directly to the question of what structure predictors learn versus memorize.

Bohan Liu, Xiaohan Fan, Wenqian Ye, Aidong Zhang

arXiv:2610.36226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structure predictors like ESMFold fold proteins using neural network computation and have transformed structural biology. However, the driving mechanism from amino-acid (AA) sequence to 3D structure is insufficiently understood, and biological meaning remains locked in the dense network. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promising results in obtaining interpretable concept features over an overcomplete basis of intermediate protein sequence-model representations. Yet folding models, which predict physical shape from AA sequence semantics, have no such account. We hypothesize that the features carrying the folding computation evolve in the 3D structural regression process. In this paper, we interpret the folding trunk in three steps. First, a pilot analysis on the representation distribution across modules and recycles locates distinct spatial computation in the trunk. Second, the dictionaries expose a division of labor: the single representation carries inherited semantics, and the pair representation computes the pairwise geometry. Third, we interpret the dictionary at scale with a reasoning language model, trace how the concepts compose across blocks by gradient-based attribution, and follow the interpreted code to the model's folding output, verifying where the computation aligns with, or departs from, known biochemistry. Together, the sparse dictionaries we train capture the relational geometry the trunk computes beyond the sequence model, and their concept activations forecast the model's own fold quality, turning the black-box folding trunk into a sparse, interpretable, and scientifically verifiable circuit.

item.title: [7] Accurate structural modelling of protein-glycan recognition with GlycoWeave
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

GlycoWeave is a diffusion model sampling glycan poses in internal-coordinate space and reports 71.9% top-25 success against 19.2% for AlphaFold 3 on 698 complexes, a pointed benchmark of a cofolding failure mode with a chemically constrained sampler.

Huifeng Zhao, Jintu Zhang, Yifei Xiao, Youqiao Qian, Silong Zhai, Zichang Jin, Li Wang, Yuchao Wang, Hang Dong, Yifan Zhao, Zhenxing Wu, Hongyan Du, Yuansheng Huang, Bowei Zhao, Xiaorui Wang, Shukai Gu, Jike Wang, Zhongjun Li, Zhongtang Li, Tingjun Hou, Yu Kang

arXiv:2610.37410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein-glycan recognition underlies diverse biological processes, yet accurate prediction of protein-glycan complex structures remains challenging owing to the chemical diversity, conformational flexibility and sparse experimental structural coverage of glycans. Here we present GlycoWeave, a glycan-specific diffusion framework that integrates chemically constrained conformational sampling, multiscale molecular representations and multi-source learning. By operating in internal-coordinate space, GlycoWeave preserves glycan connectivity and stereochemistry while efficiently exploring bound conformations. A heterogeneous equivariant network couples atom-level interaction geometry with monosaccharide-level structural context, whereas multi-source, multi-head training integrates experimental complexes with structures refined using classical and quantum mechanics-informed potentials. On a benchmark of 698 protein-glycan complexes, GlycoWeave achieves a 71.9% Top-25 high-quality success rate, compared with 19.2% for AlphaFold 3, while requiring only 0.34 s per sampled pose. GlycoWeave further preserves glycan structural validity, recovers native protein-glycan interactions and reproduces linkage-specific conformational preferences, maintaining high accuracy across diverse glycan architectures and protein environments. These results establish GlycoWeave as an accurate, efficient and chemically faithful framework for modelling protein-glycan recognition. GlycoWeave is freely available at https://cadd.zju.edu.cn/glycoweave.

item.title: [8] Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Epitope excision cuts RFdiffusion and AlphaFold3 GPU time by up to 88% on large targets, and an agentic loop (human-in-the-loop versus fully autonomous, with yeast-display validation) is an unusually serious evaluation of agents running a structural design workflow.

Jun W. Kim, Artiom Myaskovsky, Oscar Donosa, Lawrence Chan, Jamie Rogers, Avinatan Hassidim, Yossi Matias, Annalisa Pawlosky

arXiv:2610.33195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: De novo protein design campaigns remain bottlenecked by the inference compute time required to generate and rank candidates, limiting wider functional exploration. Here, we introduce and evaluate an epitope excision approach that truncates targets to local interface windows to accelerate both backbone diffusion and structure prediction. Across 15 targets and 3,666 designs, excised windows closely reproduced full-target binding interfaces (median C\alpha RMSD of 0.37 \AA) and made it practical to design binders against the 719-residue extracellular domain of fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) by cutting RFdiffusion and AlphaFold3 GPU time by ~ 88% in one of the epitopes. Pairing this workflow with an agentic optimization loop allowed the system to autonomously identify catalytic-site targeting strategies. Under a fixed compute budget, a human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflow raised the computational hit rate from 5.06% to 9.33% while further cutting GPU hours by ~ 42%. We also found that omitting target multiple sequence alignments during refolding roughly substantially increased the apparent yield. Wet-lab validation with yeast display identified nanomolar binders from the generated designs with the HITL and the fully autonomous agent (human-out-of-the-loop, HOOTL) arms recovering more enriched designs than the PI-alone baseline. Together, target excision and agent-guided search offer a practical way to scale de novo binder design to large, therapeutically relevant proteins.

item.title: [8] Can Folding Models Tell Binders from Bluffers? Evidence from POISK: The Patent-Derived Antibody Dataset
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

This is a 22k-complex benchmark of Boltz-2, OpenFold3, Protenix-v1/v2 and AF-Multimer on whether cofolding confidence separates true binders from decoys, with leakage-aware data and an epitope-localization failure analysis that bears directly on how much to trust these models.

Tupikina, D., Roncoli, A., Bujotzek, A., Abanades, B.

Structure prediction models are increasingly deployed as zero-shot digital screens in antibody design, operating under the assumption that high folding confidence implies true binding. However, rigorous validation of this premise has been limited by small test sets, narrow target diversity, and the risk of data leakage from training-adjacent structures. Here we introduce POISK: Patent-extracted Organization of Immunoglobulin Sequence Knowledge, a large-scale dataset derived from the US patent literature, comprising 89074 antibody-antigen records extracted from 10110 patents using an LLM-based pipeline. From this resource, we curate a balanced benchmark set of 22494 complexes: 11247 patent-validated binders without a known resolved structure paired with putative non-binders constructed from sequence-similar human repertoire antibodies. Using this dataset, we benchmark six leading structure prediction models (AlphaFold-Multimer, Boltz-2, IntelliFold v2, OpenFold3, Protenix-v1, and Protenix-v2) on their ability to discriminate binders from decoys. The best-performing model, Protenix-v2, achieves 72% pairwise accuracy over all pairs and 87% on the most confident half of predictions, and correctly identifies the true binder from a pool of 50 candidates in 29% of trials; this represents a substantial enrichment over random selection, yet remains far from reliable single-candidate identification. Structural consensus across models also discriminates binders from decoys, with pairwise accuracy reaching 73.1% when three or more models converge on a pose (DockQ>0.23, covering around 54.2% of pairs). Epitope localization remains unreliable: the best model contacts annotated epitope residues in only 62.8% of cases, indicating that binding discrimination does not establish accurate epitope localization. Our results suggest that current folding models provide useful but limited signal for antibody screening and should be complemented by orthogonal methods. We release POISK as a community resource for future benchmarking and model training.

item.title: [7] NUViT: Vision Transformers for Fourier Space Data
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Zhong lab's NUViT builds a transformer that respects Fourier-space structure and tests it on cryo-EM heterogeneity analysis, directly touching the cryo-EM heterogeneity modeling you care about.

Jeffrey Gu, Robert C. Heeter, Ellen D. Zhong

arXiv:2610.32041v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated strong performance in many computer vision tasks but do not naturally extend beyond the natural image domain. One important example is Fourier-space data, which is used to represent a rich and diverse set of modalities, including medical imaging and microscopy. Standard ViT tokenization partitions an image into square patches on a Cartesian grid, which poorly fit the frequency and phase structure of Fourier-space data. We introduce Non-Uniform ViT, a simple, general-purpose vision transformer that redesigns image tokenization, data representation, and positional encoding to respect this structure. Experiments on Fourier-domain image classification, 2D crystal lattice identification, MRI annotation, and cryo-EM protein heterogeneity analysis show that NUViT consistently captures the structure of Fourier data better than standard architectures.

item.title: [7] Provably Reliable Classifier Guidance via Cross-Entropy Control
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

This gives the first quantitative guarantee linking classifier cross-entropy to classifier-guidance error in diffusion models, which is directly useful theory for reasoning about when learned guidance signals steer reliably.

Sharan Sahu, Arisina Banerjee, Yuchen Wu

arXiv:2601.21200v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Classifier-guided diffusion models generate conditional samples by augmenting the reverse-time score with the gradient of the log-probability predicted by a probabilistic classifier. In practice, this classifier is usually obtained by minimizing an empirical loss function. While existing statistical theory guarantees good generalization performance when the sample size is sufficiently large, it remains unclear whether such training yields an effective guidance mechanism. We study this question in the context of cross-entropy loss, which is widely used for classifier training. Under mild smoothness assumptions on the classifier, we show that controlling the cross-entropy at each diffusion model step is sufficient to control the corresponding guidance error. In particular, probabilistic classifiers achieving conditional KL divergence $\varepsilon^2$ induce guidance vectors with mean squared error $\widetilde O(d \varepsilon )$, up to constant and logarithmic factors. Our result yields an upper bound on the sampling error of classifier-guided diffusion models and bears resemblance to a reverse log-Sobolev--type inequality. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result that quantitatively links classifier training to guidance alignment in diffusion models, providing both a theoretical explanation for the empirical success of classifier guidance, and principled guidelines for selecting classifiers that induce effective guidance.

item.title: [7] Unliganded Active State of the β2-Adrenergic Receptor Revealed by Pressure-Resolved DEER and ProGuide Molecular Modeling
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Pressure-resolved DEER combined with ProGuide biased MD maps an otherwise hidden unliganded active state of the beta2AR, which is experimental-data-restrained conformational ensemble modeling directly parallel to your steering-with-data theme.

Lerch, M., Brennan, P. C., Garces, A. M., Grosskopf, J. D. et al.

The intrinsic ability of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), such as the {beta}2-adrenergic receptor ({beta}2AR), to sample an ensemble of distinct conformational states with varying affinities and catalytic activities for intracellular transducers such as G proteins and {beta} arrestins is a feature that underlies their signaling complexity. The structural features of the full ensemble of accessible conformations remain largely inaccessible to conventional biophysical techniques due to the low populations of transient or intermediate states. Here, we integrate pressure-resolved double electron electron resonance (PR DEER) with the ProGuide biased molecular dynamics framework to map elusive {beta}2AR conformations obscured under ambient conditions. Our results demonstrate a pressure dependent, global two-state equilibrium between inactive- and active-like conformations in the unliganded receptor and indicate a high degree of allosteric coupling among transmembrane helices in the absence of ligand binding. Notably, {beta}2AR bound to the superagonist BI 167107 samples a smaller conformational space than the unliganded active conformation revealed by pressure, suggesting that this agonist constrains {beta}2AR to a more restricted subset of conformers within the active ensemble. This finding points towards a conformational selection mechanism of activation of the {beta}2AR wherein signaling variability exists because of conformational heterogeneity within the active state.

item.title: [9] Beyond Best-of-$k$: Prior-Consistent DAPS for Ambiguous Nonlinear Inverse Problems
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

Prior-consistent DAPS directly tackles your core problem of diffusion posterior sampling for ambiguous nonlinear inverse problems like phase retrieval (the crystallographic phase problem), and exposes how best-of-k evaluation hides prior-inconsistent solutions.

Merve Kocabas, Benjamin A. Burns, Andreas Geiger, Kent Gauen, Sara Fridovich-Keil

arXiv:2610.31592v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion models have become strong priors for solving inverse problems. However, nonlinear inverse problems such as phase retrieval remain challenging when multiple measurement-consistent solutions are distinguishable only by the prior; we call such measurements ambiguous. Existing diffusion-based samplers rely on local approximations during reconstruction. For an ambiguous measurement, these approximations can allow measurement guidance to favor a measurement-consistent mode that is close to a prior-supported mode but is itself not supported by the prior. Evaluation often masks this type of failure by reporting the best-of-$k$ runs, where the best is selected by comparison to the ground truth. We introduce Prior-Consistent DAPS (PC-DAPS), a variant of Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling (DAPS) designed to address this failure case by maintaining multiple candidate solutions within a single sampling run. As annealing noise decreases, PC-DAPS prunes and replaces weaker candidates according to their prior consistency, without any ground-truth access. PC-DAPS reduces the incidence of prior-inconsistent samples and improves sample quality on nonlinear inverse problems while preserving sample quality and diversity on linear inverse problems.

item.title: [7] MutaStruct: Revisiting Benchmarks for Single-Site Mutation-Induced Structural Change Prediction
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

MutaStruct shows that a Copy-WT control stays competitive on backbone metrics while rankings shift on mutation-site metrics, which is a pointed critique of whether structure predictors capture mutation-induced conformational change rather than memorizing the wild type.

Huynh, T.-P., Ho, D.-M., Nguyen, V. T. D., Kha, Q.-H. et al.

Predicting the structural consequences of single-site mutations is fundamental to understanding protein function, disease mechanisms, and protein engineering. However, existing benchmarks for mutation-induced structural change prediction are often affected by duplicate mutation events, highly similar structural pairs, and experimental-state confounders, which can inflate reported performance. We introduce MutaStruct, a curated benchmark of experimentally observed single-mutation protein structure pairs designed for rigorous evaluation of mutation-induced structural changes. MutaStruct combines residue-level sequence validation, coordinate-level quality control, context-aware filtering, event-level deduplication, and leakage-aware data splitting to improve dataset reliability and evaluation rigor. We benchmark sequence-only structure prediction, physics-based refinement, and learning-based refinement methods together with a Copy-WT diagnostic control. Copy-WT remains highly competitive on backbone-based metrics, while method rankings change substantially across local and mutation-site measures. These results show that overall structural fidelity does not necessarily imply accurate modeling of mutation-associated structural change, underscoring the need for further methodological development beyond current paradigms. The benchmark dataset is currently undergoing further curation and expansion and will be released in a future journal-version update. The codebase, trained models, and evaluation pipeline are publicly available at https://github.com/HySonLab/MutaStruct

item.title: [9] QUBO-Based Conformer Selection with Quantum-Classical Hybrid Optimization for Multiconformer Ligand Modeling
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

Directly reformulates qFit-ligand multiconformer selection as a QUBO and benchmarks it against the MIQP baseline on 83 X-ray ligand entries using composite-omit map RSCC and EDIAm, including the notable finding that map agreement and atom-level density support diverge.

Jiyun Lee, Haeseong Kim, Junho Lee, Joonsuk Huh

arXiv:2610.29058v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A ligand can adopt multiple conformations within the same binding site, and these conformations can interact differently with the surrounding protein. Multiconformer modeling must therefore determine which candidate conformations to retain and what occupancies to assign to them. An established automated approach uses mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) with hard occupancy and conformer-count limits for this selection. Here, we reformulated conformer selection as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem with finite penalties and discrete occupancies. We solved the QUBO using a quantum-classical hybrid solver. We compared this workflow with the MIQP-based qFit-ligand workflow across 83 paired X-ray ligand entries using the same experimental inputs and the same qFit-ligand processing protocol. For each entry, both final models were evaluated against the same composite-omit map generated from the common input structure before the two workflows diverged. Quantum-qFit produced higher ligand-region real-space correlation coefficients (RSCC) in 62 entries 74.7% and lower occupancy-weighted torsional strain in 66 entries 79.5%. Similar directional trends remained in the 28 entries with matched final conformer counts. The molecular Electron Density for Individual Atoms score (EDIAm) decreased in most entries. This result shows that higher regional map agreement did not necessarily correspond to stronger atom-level density support. Overall, the results show that the conformer-selection formulation can change which ligand states are represented from the same experimental data and provide a QUBO framework for studying multiconformer ligand selection.

item.title: [8] Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Proposes a new training-free route to reward-tilted diffusion sampling by evaluating the base denoiser at shifted, rescaled inputs rather than adding drift terms, which is a genuinely new guidance idea even though it is shown on discrete hypercube data.

Curtis McDonald, Peter Bartlett

arXiv:2610.29086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reward guidance methods sample an exponential tilt of a base density using a diffusion model trained with only samples from the base distribution. Existing methods use what we call external guidance: additive terms in the drift or multiplicative terms on the transition probabilities. We propose internal guidance which leaves the output of the base denoiser unmodified and instead changes the point at which it is evaluated. For discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube $\{-1,1\}^{d}$, the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input. In practice the base denoiser is a neural network trained on noised samples of the base distribution. The required evaluation points for sampling the tilted density would be out-of-distribution for basic noising of the base distribution. We modify the training algorithm with random diagonal rescalings of the data, so that the denoiser network learns both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations of the denoiser relative to the base distribution. A single denoiser network samples binary reward tilts, class labels, and infilling with no fine-tuning and no external guidance term.

item.title: [8] DEEP: Extracting Latent Energetic Landscapes from Protein Structure Predictors
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

DEEP extracts statistical potentials from Boltz-2's own distograms and shows these cofolding models encode energetic information that AlphaFold2 lacks, bearing directly on what Boltz learns versus memorizes and on using it as a prior for conformations.

Rozsa, Z. B., Erdos, G.

Modern protein structure predictors learn complex sequence-structure relationships, yet the extent to which their internal representations capture the energetic principles governing protein stability and conformational preferences remains unclear. Here, we introduce DEEP (Distogram Encoded Energetic Potential), a general framework that extracts effective statistical potentials directly from predicted residue-pair distance distributions, using the models own terminal distance state as an internal reference without training on experimental stability data. Applied to Boltz-2 (DEEP-Boltz) achieves a mean per-assay Spearman correlation of 0.720 across 64 ProteinGym stability assays, numerically outperforming all 97 published zero-shot methods in the matched comparison on level with the best performing predictors trained directly on experimental stability measurements. Beyond mutation effects, DEEP-Boltz accurately distinguishes native-like from non-native conformations across more than 180,000 Rosetta decoys. Applying DEEP to AlphaFold2 reveals nearly identical conformational discrimination but substantially weaker mutation-effect prediction, demonstrating that recognizing favorable conformations and capturing their energetic sensitivity to sequence changes are distinct properties of learned structural representations. Together, these findings establish that protein structure predictors encode accessible energetic information beyond their geometric predictions and that this information can be extracted. We release the framework and DEEP-Boltz as a freely available tool for extracting these latent energetic representations and for zero-shot prediction of mutation-induced protein stability changes.

item.title: [7] Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Single-observation flow-matching posterior estimators combined only at inference time to co-refine X-ray and neutron data is a direct template for fusing multiple experimental restraints in a generative prior, though applied to thin-film reflectometry rather than biomolecules.

Valentin Munteanu, Alexander Hinderhofer, Dmitry Lapkin, Vladimir Starostin, Frank Schreiber

arXiv:2610.29362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.

item.title: [7] Multi-Objective Protein Optimization via Modular Diffusion Steering
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Modular inference-time diffusion steering with scalar rewards that can be paired with different diffusion models and steering procedures closely mirrors the plug-in guidance architecture of your sampleworks platform, applied to protein optimization, though it builds on existing steering methods.

Meir Roketlishvili, Felix Huber, Wenda Chu, Yisong Yue, Raul Astudillo

arXiv:2610.28943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein engineering often requires improving several properties simultaneously, motivating the search for high-performing sequences that represent useful fitness tradeoffs. Discovering these sequences is challenging because the design space is combinatorially large and experimental campaigns often permit only a few rounds of batched measurements. We introduce \textit{MODS}, a modular framework for multi-objective protein optimization via inference-time diffusion steering. For each proposal, MODS samples augmented Chebyshev scalarization weights and a fitness-surrogate ensemble member to define a scalar steering reward. Varying the weights directs generation toward different objective tradeoffs, while varying ensemble members diversifies the predictions used for guidance. Because MODS expresses multi-objective acquisition through scalar rewards, it can be paired with different diffusion models and compatible steering procedures. After each evaluation batch, MODS updates the surrogates without retraining the generative model. We evaluate MODS on six protein optimization tasks using predictive oracles trained on experimental assay data, with two diffusion models and two steering procedures. MODS achieves competitive final hypervolume across all six tasks with both diffusion models, and substantially outperforms the best evaluated baseline on several tasks. Our results demonstrate a flexible and effective approach to multi-objective protein optimization with limited feedback.
